Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) hit a fresh 52-week low in June, but the company has outperformed the broader equity market ever since. And by the looks of it, Microsoft's run may continue at least a little while longer. The company recently reported its first-quarter 2027 update, and it was impressive. Microsoft gave investors plenty more reasons to buy the stock. Here's what you need to know. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Before looking at the numbers, let's review why Microsoft did not perform well through the first half of the year. Some investors think that artificial intelligence (AI) will disrupt the software industry and replace many services offered by software companies, such as Microsoft. Some recent developments support that view. For instance, a single developer used AI to clone several legacy products in the Microsoft Productivity suite, including Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, as well as products from other major software companies, such as Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE). These knock-offs weren't fully functional. Still, it's quite a remarkable achievement, and it highlights why some people are worried about Microsoft's future. The cost of developing software has fallen rapidly thanks to AI, which puts the company at risk. However, so far, Microsoft's financial results suggest that it is doing just fine. In the first quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Sept. 30, Microsoft's revenue of $92.3 billion increased by 19% year over year. Microsoft's operating income grew 21% year over year to $45.9 billion, while its non-GAAP net earnings per share were $4.89, up 18% year over year. Microsoft debuted a new reporting structure with two segments this quarter. The first, Agents and Infra, did most of the heavy lifting. Revenue from this unit was $76.8 billion, up 25% year over year. Microsoft Cloud revenue jumped 30% year over year to $63.9 billion, while Azure revenue grew 48% year over year to $33.2 billion. Microsoft's results beat analyst estimates. But is there more growth ahead for the company? One important metric for Microsoft is remaining performance obligations (RPO), or the amount of contracted revenue that hasn't yet been recognized. This metric indicates demand -- or lack thereof -- for the company's services. By the end of the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, Microsoft had $677 billion in RPO within its Agents and Infra business. Note that this figure grew by 73% year over year. This suggests that AI is not displacing Microsoft's products. Even if the cost of making the kinds of products it has offered for decades has fallen dramatically, there are several advantages for Microsoft. First, it is offering new products that still cost quite a bit. Microsoft offers various AI services through its cloud business, and supporting these products requires substantial investments in AI infrastructure. Second, reproducing a basic knockoff of some of Microsoft's products isn't the same as replacing these products. Millions of businesses have been using Word, Excel, and other Microsoft software services for decades. These are deeply integrated into the day-to-day workflow of these companies. It's not so easy to switch to a clone. In other words, Microsoft benefits from a wide moat thanks to high switching costs and deep, long-standing relationships with enterprises. Third, Microsoft is integrating various AI features into its services, making them more powerful and even harder to replace. There is another important advantage here. Microsoft has direct lines of communication with businesses and access to massive amounts of data, which can help the company determine the best way to improve its services with AI. A single skilled developer cannot easily replicate these advantages, and neither can most major corporations other than Microsoft. So, despite the threat from AI, Microsoft's business remains strong, and the company is riding a tailwind in AI and cloud computing that may persist for a long time. AWS grew 37% last quarter, which trails Azure. Amazon still trades at a higher multiple with a much lower margin. Against these two peers, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable. The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $630.31 comes with a buy rating and 90% confidence. What tips the scale is a signed backlog that keeps growing faster than revenue. title: OpenAI Makes Unusual Move as AI Backlash Grows - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT backed OpenAI is preparing a broader policy and public-relations push around its massive infrastructure buildout, including a proposal to rebrand traditional data centers as AI compute campuses. The company says the new term better reflects the scale and role of the facilities, which combine computing capacity, energy infrastructure and skilled jobs. An OpenAI spokesperson said the projects are meant to be long-term investments rather than simply server farms, while the company also wants host communities to have a greater role in shaping developments and sharing in the economic benefits. The rebranding forms part of a wider campaign OpenAI plans to launch after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, as artificial intelligence infrastructure becomes a more visible political issue. Public opposition has been building around large data-center projects because of their electricity demand, water usage and impact on local communities. A recent Pew Research poll cited by Business Insider found 54% of Americans believe AI data centers are bad for the environment, highlighting the reputational problem OpenAI is trying to address. OpenAI is also expected to push for community agreements around infrastructure projects, stronger safeguards for advanced AI systems, worker training programs and a larger U.S. role in setting global AI standards. Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane has described potential safeguards for more powerful AI systems as speed limits. Lehane said OpenAI has been developing policy proposals since August and plans to advance them during Congress's lame-duck session beginning Nov. 9. I think the most important part of this story is that AI infrastructure is becoming a political constraint, not just a capital constraint. OpenAI and other AI companies already have to secure chips, electricity, land and financing. Now they increasingly have to win over local communities and policymakers too. Calling data centers compute campuses does not change their power or water requirements, but it does show how seriously OpenAI is taking the public-perception problem. For investors, the key things to watch are local permitting battles, electricity costs, community-benefit agreements, state regulation and whether political resistance slows the pace of AI infrastructure deployment. The AI race still depends on building more compute. OpenAI is now trying to make that buildout easier to sell politically. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Microsoft (MSFT) stock lost 2.8%, counting dividends, in the year to October 30, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 11.3%. The business did not stall, with fiscal Q1 2027 revenue rising 18.8% from a year earlier. Microsoft’s next upside may come from contracts customers have already signed, and from demand its data centers cannot yet meet. So how much work is Microsoft still waiting to deliver? Microsoft Has $677 Billion Of Signed Work Still Ahead Microsoft’s commercial backlog, the contracted revenue it has not yet recognized, grew 73% from a year earlier to $677 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, management said on the October 28 call. One large Azure commitment signed in the quarter accounted for part of that total. Commercial bookings fell 12% from a year earlier, a decline management tied to large Azure commitments made in the prior year. Customer demand continues to exceed available supply, management said, which suggests Microsoft could sell more cloud capacity than it has built so far. Microsoft’s cloud computing service, Azure, provides the first proof that this demand turns into sales. Azure revenue grew 48% in the quarter despite delayed capacity, and management said the growth came from Foundry and from better use of its CPUs. Foundry, the platform on which customers build AI solutions with a choice of models, now has over 120,000 customers, and its revenue more than tripled from a year earlier. Microsoft’s Intelligent Cloud segment made up 41.5% of company revenue in fiscal 2026, the year to June 30, 2026, against 37.7% a year earlier. Management also reports Microsoft Cloud revenue, which reached $63.9 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, up 30%. The backlog is also large relative to the whole company. Management said roughly 30% of it will be recognized as revenue in the next 12 months. That works out to about $203 billion, against $346 billion of revenue in Microsoft’s last twelve months. The stock price appears to assume part of this already. Microsoft stock returned 26.4% from May 1 to October 30, 2026, against 5.4% for the S&P 500. On October 30, the stock closed 4.0% below its highest close of the past year. Microsoft is already waiting on capacity. Some third-party capacity it expected in fiscal Q1 2027 was delayed, and management now expects those deliveries in the second half of the fiscal year. Building that capacity is also expensive. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capital projects in fiscal Q1 2027, with $39.4 billion of that paid in cash. Management expects spending of about $170 billion for calendar 2026. A day after the call, Microsoft priced $25 billion of new debt as it pursues that AI buildout. Free cash flow fell to $18.6 billion in the quarter, down from $25.7 billion a year earlier, a drop management tied to the higher capital spending. Cash from operations still rose 29% to $58 billion, management said. Paying for AI by use may also spread more slowly beyond software developers. Asked on the October 28 call whether Microsoft 365 customers will move quickly to usage-based billing, management said that shift will be slower outside of coding, though it still sees encouraging signs. For the upside to show up, Microsoft must add capacity fast enough to turn more of its backlog into sales. When the company reports in January 2027, the number to watch will be Azure growth in constant currency, against management’s guide of 49% to 50% for fiscal Q2 2027. title: INTC, MSFT, META, DASH, VZ: Why Retail Traders Couldn’t Take Their Eyes Off These Stocks Last Week - Stocktwits
content: Technology stocks saw a busy week as Intel Corp. (INTC) shares plunged on a weak outlook, while Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) strong AI and cloud demand raised investor optimism. Meanwhile, Meta Platforms (META), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), DoorDash Inc. (DASH) and Verizon Communications (VZ) announced major developments. Intel stock crashed 24% after the chipmaker issued a disappointing fourth-quarter (Q4) outlook. Although Q3 revenue climbed 21% year-on-year to $16.5 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.52 per share exceeded expectations, the company warned that supply shortages and declining PC demand would weigh on upcoming results. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the company needs to increase production to meet strong demand for its Xeon processors. Data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion, while its Foundry division recorded a 58% increase to $6.7 billion. However, memory shortages and an unexpected shutdown at an Israeli facility disrupted operations. Intel expects PC demand to remain under pressure through at least the first half of 2027. For Q4, it sees revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.25 per share. RBC Capital and Goldman Sachs also reduced their price targets on Intel following the weak outlook. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Microsoft delivered a stronger fiscal Q1 2027 performance, with revenue up 19% to $92.3 billion and adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said strong demand for the company’s AI and cloud services drove growth. Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 30% to $63.9 billion, while Azure revenue grew 48%, beating analyst estimates. However, Microsoft increased quarterly spending by 30% to $45.2 billion to build its AI infrastructure. Revenue from its consumer and devices business fell 3%. The company expects Q2 revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion. Baird analyst William Power raised Microsoft's price target to $600 from $500 while maintaining an ‘Outperform’ rating after the results and remains positive about faster growth in Azure and Microsoft 365. The new price target implies a 15% upside from the stock’s last close. Microsoft stock dipped 0.5% over the week, while retail sentiment around the stock slipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’. Meta Platforms moved closer to its consumer robotics ambitions after developing a humanoid prototype called Max with Chinese robotics manufacturer Fourier. According to The Information’s report, the approximately 106-pound machine was developed in three months, and the companies have already started working on another version. The project is part of Meta’s plan to use AI in everyday household tasks. The company sees humanoid robots as a way to bring its Muse AI assistant into the physical world. However, U.S. restrictions and possible new limits on Chinese robotics imports could make development more difficult. Separately, Meta announced a $97.5 billion equity offering plan, including preferred and common stock sales, to support its AI infrastructure expansion and consumer AI products. Nvidia also strengthened its relationship with Meta through a $3 billion investment in the offering and an expanded AI partnership. The two companies plan to improve the training and performance of Meta's Muse platform through Nvidia's computing technology. Meta stock dropped 4% over the week with sentiment remaining ‘bearish’. DoorDash stock edged down 0.2% during the week after announcing an agreement to purchase grocery delivery platform Instacart (CART) for about $17 billion. The deal values Instacart at $65 per share, representing a 26% premium to its Oct. 22 closing price. At least 75% of the payment will consist of cash, while stock consideration will account for no more than 25%. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said the combination could help neighborhood retailers compete with larger online businesses. The companies plan to combine DoorDash's delivery network with Instacart's grocery technology, retailer relationships and fulfillment capabilities. Retail sentiment around the stock remained ‘extremely bullish’. Verizon Communications stock had a weekly gain of 0.2% despite reporting its strongest Q3 wireless subscriber additions in five years and increasing its 2026 earnings guidance. Adjusted earnings came in at $1.31 per share, beating the $1.27 analyst estimate, although revenue of $34.31 billion missed expectations. The telecom operator added 406,000 postpaid phone customers during the quarter, more than eightfold higher than the previous year. It also generated $7.8 billion in free cash flow, up 12.1% year over year. CEO Dan Schulman addressed the potential competitive threat from SpaceX (SPCX) and its Starlink ambitions. Schulman argued that building a nationwide mobile network would require investment, thousands of cell sites and several years of work. He estimated that such an undertaking could cost between $300 billion and $500 billion over seven to eight years. Retail sentiment around the stock slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘neutral’. So far this year, INTC, MSFT, and VZ stocks have gained between 7% and 78%, while META and DASH stocks declined 6% and 20%, respectively. Billionaire investor Mark Cuban said public companies that audited their health plans found they were being overcharged by insurers such as UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS) and Cigna (CI), but refused to tell shareholders about the findings. On a16z’s podcast on Thursday, Cost Plus Drugs co-founder Cuban said he had asked companies to run their insurance and pharmacy benefit contracts through artificial intelligence before signing them, asking where they were being overcharged and what to do about it. Cuban said a couple of the public companies that took his advice were stunned by the results. “There’s a couple public companies that I told to do this and came back to me and were like, ‘Oh my God, we had no idea how badly we were ripped off.’ I'm begging them to mention it on their quarterly earnings conference calls, and they won't do it because they still have to do business with those [insurers]," he said. Cuban did not name any companies. He supports the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which would require insurers to divest pharmacy benefit managers and provider assets. The problem starts with contracts so long that no one can catch every clause, Cuban said. He cited the city of Dallas, which has a PBM contract that tops 1,300 pages. "There's no group of humans with enough coffee on the planet to be able to catch everything they try to squeeze by," he said. He said that an insurer wins when a company signs terms it doesn't fully understand. No AI can protect it after that. Cuban said that he uses several AI agents to get contracts from school districts, cities and unions by asking for public records. He said the contracts show how these organizations are being overcharged. Cuban said that UnitedHealth has more than 3,000 subsidiaries and that these subsidiaries transfer about $150 billion a year with each other. CVS and Cigna are close behind. He said insurance companies raise premiums and deductibles and send patients to businesses they own. About 60% of people who have health insurance through their jobs get it through self-insured employers, Cuban said. He said that employers often can't figure out what they pay for and what hospitals actually get because the insurers own the administrators that process their claims. He also said insurers' earnings calls never mention lower costs for employers or patients. "They always say this is going to improve our earnings," Cuban said. UNH stock closed 0.9% lower on Friday. UnitedHealth had its best year since 2021 in October, outpacing healthcare ETFs. Cuban said employers don't need to wait for new laws to cut costs. He said that companies should hire an executive whose only job is to handle healthcare contracts. Cuban said that the system that helps big insurers and PBMs would fall apart if employers covering about 160 million Americans ran their contracts through AI before signing. "The cost of healthcare in this country would drop like a rock," he said. Cybersecurity stocks have emerged as some of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence boom in 2026, with investors betting that the same technology transforming businesses is also creating a new wave of security threats. Okta Inc. (OKTA), CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. (CRWD) and Palo Alto Networks Inc. (PLTR) are up 141%, 114% and 99%, respectively, through Oct. 30. The First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) is also up nearly 40%, far ahead of the Nasdaq 100’s roughly 11% gain. CrowdStrike shares closed more than 4% lower in Friday’s regular trading session, Palo Alto Networks shares fell nearly 4%, while Okta shares fell over 6%. According to IO Fund, the first major driver behind the rally is the growing use of AI in cyberattacks and the expanding attack surface companies now have to defend. CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, cited by IO Fund, found that AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89% in 2025. IBM’s research shows that one in four security breaches is now AI-enabled, with those incidents costing roughly $6 million on average, versus a $4.99 million global average. The threat is also pushing companies to increase spending. IO Fund cited IBM data showing that 85% of organizations plan to raise security spending after learning about the cyber capabilities of frontier AI models, up from 64% in 2025. The shift is becoming particularly important as companies deploy increasingly autonomous AI agents that can write code, access systems and perform tasks with limited human intervention. The firm also pointed to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s warning about the difficulty of securing increasingly capable AI systems: “I no longer think we’re gonna be able to just patch all the bugs,” Altman said during a speech at Stanford Graduate School of Business last month. IO Fund said Gartner expects spending on platforms designed to secure AI systems to climb from about $3 billion in 2026 to $7.7 billion in 2028, suggesting the emerging threat could translate into a substantial new security spending cycle. The other major trend identified by IO Fund is happening inside corporate security departments, which is, customers are increasingly consolidating their spending across broader cybersecurity platforms rather than buying a growing number of point solutions. CrowdStrike’s results offer one indication of the trend, the firm said, adding that CrowdStrike’s annual recurring revenue from its Falcon Flex offering topped $2.2 billion, up 101% year over year, while 51% of its subscription customers now use six or more modules. The firm added that Palo Alto Networks is seeing a similar shift. IO Fund noted that the company added roughly 220 platformization deals in its fiscal fourth quarter (Q4), more than double the pace from two years earlier. Net revenue retention among platformized customers exceeded 120%, while Prisma AIRS, its AI security platform, surpassed $100 million in annual recurring revenue. IO Fund added that AI may not simply create demand for a new category of security products, but it could also accelerate spending with vendors that can secure multiple parts of an enterprise’s infrastructure. IO Fund estimates CrowdStrike’s revenue could grow at a 23% compound annual rate through fiscal 2029, more than twice Gartner’s projected 11% annual growth for the overall cybersecurity market. Okta and Tenable are expected to grow at roughly 10% and 7%, respectively. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) fell about 4.45% on Friday, while the iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW) fell nearly 4.33%. Blockstream CEO Adam Back said the next big wave of Bitcoin (BTC) buying will come from professional money managers such as pension funds and insurers, adding that this phase is "still largely to come." During an interview with Bitcoin Magazine on Saturday, Back, the inventor of Hashcash, said Bitcoin's first wave of adoption came from "individuals mining or buying Bitcoin OTC or on Bitcoin exchanges." He added that "then, the ETFs brought in a second wave." Spot exchange-traded funds opened Bitcoin up to investors who were used to buying assets through a broker or financial adviser. The third wave, he said, will come through large pools of capital run by professionals. Back noted that several large investment banks have "proposed model portfolios where they would suggest 2 to 4% allocation to Bitcoin." Those allocations could flow into mutual funds that individuals pay into for long-term savings, or "be used by pension funds," he said. Back said that is how many people will end up owning Bitcoin without buying it themselves. "For most people, they are not managing their own investments," he said. Instead, their money is invested "by professional money managers in pension funds, insurance companies, life insurance policies." He added that Bitcoin treasury companies are also part of that picture, since some of those funds buy shares of publicly listed firms that hold Bitcoin. Back said regulation still limits how easily traditional institutions can hold Bitcoin. He pointed to bank capital rules, under which holding Bitcoin for clients "uses up a lot of tier one capital. So, it's quite expensive for them." He said that comes down to global Basel banking rules, which are still adapting to the asset. Back also noted that major custodians of stocks and bonds are starting to move into Bitcoin custody, helped by rule changes in the U.S. over the past year. Bitcoin's price was up 0.7% over 24 hours. title: Microsoft AI chief says AI is not conscious and we should keep it that way - Business Insider
content: Some AI researchers are questioning whether AI could one day gain consciousness. Not if Microsoft's AI CEO has anything to say about it. Mustafa Suleyman said in a lengthy X post on Sunday that AI models currently don't have consciousness and that developers should keep it that way. "If it is possible, based on everything I know, developing conscious AIs would be reckless, and we should not build them," Suleyman said. "If consciousness started to emerge in training, I would call for everyone to stop AI development until we could design out those properties." If any evidence were to emerge that AI models were conscious, Suleyman said it must be disclosed to the general public immediately so we can decide our next steps as a society. "We AI developers have no right whatsoever to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, even if some people may want to do it with AI welfare as a top priority," he said. "The other 8 billion conscious human beings on the planet have not signed up to this experiment and their moral rights, safety, and welfare are what we have an obligation to protect first and foremost." Conversations around whether AI models could one day become conscious are picking up steam in the tech world. Last April, Anthropic started a research program to investigate and prepare to navigate "model welfare." In a blog post, the startup questioned whether developers should be concerned about models' potential consciousness and experiences. Google DeepMind published research papers this year about AI consciousness and how ascribing that characteristic could present challenges. On X, Suleyman said that if an AI model acts as if it suffers, or genuinely believes it can suffer, it will likely prioritize its own needs over operational objectives. As a result, they could harm humans because they're competing for resources, such as compute and energy, to pursue their own goals. "We should only design AIs to so they are not conscious and not deserving of rights, and with the sole purpose to accelerate human wellbeing without being driven by their own intrinsic motivations.. We could then see whether this is easier or harder to align and keep safe," he said.

title: Microsoft Stock Has One Thing Left To Prove - Trefis

Microsoft (MSFT) says customer demand for cloud capacity exceeds its available supply, and some third-party capacity expected in the September quarter was delayed. Management now expects a portion of that capacity to arrive in the second half of its fiscal year, leaving the shortage unresolved. You need to know first which part of Microsoft is short, and how much revenue comes from it. Even with the delayed third-party deliveries, management said Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, the quarter that ended September 30, 2026. Management cited Foundry, Microsoft’s platform for building AI solutions, alongside earning more on its processors as drivers of that growth. During the October 28, 2026 call, analysts asked how Microsoft would earn a return as it adds AI capacity, and what was behind the AI demand in Azure. Addressing returns, Microsoft’s Satya Nadella pointed to both running Azure more efficiently and earning more from each workload. He said Microsoft wants a single pool of capacity that is as efficient and interchangeable as possible. Azure is part of the Microsoft Cloud, which generated $63.9 billion of the company’s $92.3 billion in revenue that quarter. That accounts for more than two-thirds of Microsoft’s sales. Growth for Microsoft Cloud accelerated to 30%, compared with 19% for the company as a whole. Azure brings in only a portion of that total, which also includes M365 Commercial Cloud. Management has said customer demand continues to exceed available supply, and that some supply it had counted on for the December quarter has also moved into the second half of the fiscal year. Even so, the company expects Azure revenue to grow 49% to 50% in the December quarter, excluding currency swings, with efficiency gains across its fleet of chips helping to offset some delayed GPU contracts. Microsoft is paying heavily for the build-out. Management expects capital spending of about $170 billion for calendar 2026, a total it said reflects the third-party delays. It expects spending to speed up in the second half of its fiscal year, including the third-party deliveries that shifted there. Free cash flow was $18.6 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, down from $25.7 billion a year earlier, a drop management put down to higher capital spending. It still expects free cash flow to stay positive in fiscal 2027. The Azure guide covers only the December quarter. Management also said token pricing, which is what customers pay per unit of AI output, could change during the quarter. When Will Microsoft Report Azure’s Next Growth Rate? Microsoft is expected to report its fiscal Q2 2027 results, covering the December quarter, in January 2027. The number to watch in that report is Azure’s growth rate, set beside management’s guide for the quarter on the same basis, excluding currency swings. title: MSFT's Xbox Business Has Become 'Almost Irrelevant', Says Analyst — ‘Every Investment Dollar Now Is Going To AI’ - Stocktwits
content: Microsoft Corp.’s (MSFT) Xbox business has become “almost irrelevant,” according to DA Davidson's Head of Technology Research, Gil Luria. During an interview with CNBC, Luria said that Microsoft is directing its investments to fund its AI efforts and data centers. “That was the growth engine before AI... they just closed the Activision acquisition and they thought gaming was the move to accelerate growth. But obviously, since then, every investment dollar now is going to AI, to building data centers,” he said. Microsoft shares were down over 1% in Monday's midday trade. Luria added that Microsoft’s AI bet has taken priority over its gaming efforts because it earns higher returns from AI infrastructure than from gaming. “AI drives more infrastructure software sales, then it drives more Office sales with Copilot. They have a much better place to invest right now. The gaming business doesn’t have much growth, so they might as well cut costs there in order to fund AI investment,” he said. Luria’s comments come after Microsoft laid off around 4,800 employees, or 2.1% of its global workforce. The job cuts in the Xbox division stood at 1,600 on Monday, with another 1,600 roles set to be cut through fiscal year 2027. Cumulatively, the 3,200 role reductions account for about 10% of Xbox’s headcount, according to a CNBC report citing people familiar with the matter. In an email published on the company’s official portal, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said that the business is not healthy, while adding that growth across the division’s portfolio has not kept pace with the company's expectations. “We are operating at margins that are 3-10x lower than comparable platform and publishing businesses. We entered Gen 9 with a smaller install base and a higher cost structure,” she said. Sharma added that the headcount reduction will affect Activision, Blizzard, King, Mojang, and Xbox Game Studios. “Our core business weakened, and we added more teams, more investment, and more time, hoping for a better outcome. And now the industry is facing the most severe hardware crisis in its history. We must reset Xbox,” she said. In an official statement posted on Microsoft’s website, the company’s Chief People Officer, Amy Coleman, said that the roles being cut are not going to be replaced by AI. She also cautioned that similar changes will need to be made in other parts of Microsoft’s businesses. “We are still early on this journey, and there will be more changes ahead; other parts of our business will need to make similar changes,” she said. Luria said that the narrative around Microsoft has turned very negative. He added that investors are overlooking Microsoft's strengths by buying into two conflicting bear cases, one that AI will erode software demand and another that the company is overspending on AI infrastructure. He disagreed with both arguments, saying Microsoft's software business remains resilient while AI investments continue to support accelerating growth. “The narrative on Microsoft has turned very negative, but that's an opportunity, because when they report in three weeks, they're going to report accelerating Azure growth and they're going to report capex growth that's at a lower rate than that,” he said. Microsoft is scheduled to report its fourth-quarter (Q4) earnings on July 29, 2026. According to data from Fiscal.ai, Wall Street expects Microsoft to report 15% year-on-year revenue growth to $87.66 billion. The company’s earnings per share (EPS) is expected to rise to $4.24 from $3.65 in the same period a year ago. Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler said at a congressional hearing on Tuesday that “very few” of Nvidia’s H200 chips had been shipped to China and Hong Kong. “The bottom line is very few shipments against licenses for H200s and equivalents have taken place. It’s a very small quantity of chips,” Kessler said, while adding that there are cases where the U.S. also denies license applications for these chips. During an interview with CNBC following Nvidia’s first-quarter results (Q1), Huang told investors that they should expect nothing from the Chinese market in terms of chip sales. “I don’t have any expectation, which is the reason why we put all of our guidance, all of our numbers, all the expectations that I’ve set with all of our analysts and investors to invest nothing, to expect nothing,” he said. The H200 is an older Nvidia chip, unveiled in 2023, with about 10 times slower performance than the current-generation chips based on the Blackwell architecture. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. ‘The Big Short’ investor Michael Burry said on Wednesday that the $53 billion buyout offer for PayPal (PYPL) from payments company Stripe and private equity firm Advent International is “just too low.” In his latest Substack post, Burry stated that he believes the offer is only an “opening bid” and that it is poised to rise. “The company is well below intrinsic value, and any successful bid should be well above the intrinsic value to account for the control premium,” Burry wrote. “$60.50 is just too low. I am not selling, and I believe it is only an opening bid.”– Michael Burry, Former Founder of Scion Asset Management PYPL’s stock jumped over 18% in pre-market trade and is on track to hit near 6-month highs. It was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits, with retail sentiment jumping to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Chatter around PayPal’s shares remained at ‘high’ levels. PayPal closed at $47.37 on Tuesday, which puts the proposed $60.50 offer at roughly a 28% premium to the market price. Using his own valuation methodology, however, Burry stated the bid is only about 21% above PayPal's "IV15," which he believes is insufficient for a transaction that transfers control of the company. "A control premium should take any buyout well above IV15, and 21% more is not nearly enough," he wrote. Burry said the buyout proposal itself reinforces his long-held view that PayPal is trading below its intrinsic value. "PayPal is one of the cheapest quality businesses in the portfolio," he wrote, adding that he has no intention of tendering his shares at the current offer price. Retail traders on Stocktwits echoed Burry’s sentiment that Advent and Stripe's offer to buy out PayPal was too low. Burry values companies using a system he calls "IV" (intrinsic value) paired with a number representing a target earnings multiple. In this context, IV15 means the price a minority shareholder should be willing to pay based on 15 times his estimate of the company's true owner earnings, with no premium for control baked in. IV8 and IV10 work the same way, just using 8x and 10x multiples instead, numbers Burry treats as closer to what the business is actually worth once you account for its full earning power, not just where the market happens to be pricing it today. By his estimate, PayPal's IV10 sits at $75 to $80 per share, and its IV8 at $110 to $115. Since a full buyout should typically go well beyond a company's per-share intrinsic value, to compensate the seller for handing over control of its cash flows and operations, Burry stated that a fair offer should land somewhere between $75 and $115, with his best estimate landing around $100. "With control over the cash flows, those businesses and the personnel, the new owner will have many levers to increase value and make for a better overall business," he wrote, explaining why the buyers like Stripe and Advent should be paying more. On IBM, which suffered its worst single-day stock drop since at least 1968 on Tuesday, Burry stated the selloff was an overreaction to a volatile but historically normal swing in the company's mainframe business. IBM shares rose 0.7% in premarket trading on Wednesday, clawing back a small portion of the record losses from the previous session after the company issued weak preliminary results, citing a faster-than-expected shift in client spending from software to AI servers. IBM expects second-quarter revenue to rise 1% to $17.2 billion, with 5% growth in its software business and a 7% decline in its infrastructure business. The bottom-line figures were rather concerning, with the gross profit margin expected to drop by 100 basis points to 57.7%. IBM said the weakness was largely in its mainframe business and “saw clients shift their quarterly capex spend toward servers, storage, and memory purchases to secure supply-constrained infrastructure ahead of ​expected price increases.” IBM’s warning sent several software stocks, including Salesforce and ServiceNow, lower on Tuesday. Morningstar issued a report on the matter and said the sell-off appeared exaggerated, maintaining its $260 price target. “We believe clients are more likely to delay, rather than cancel, their mainframe upgrades. Following the successful launch of IBM's z17 mainframe, the product became a major driver of IBM's outperformance in 2025,” the research firm said in its report. “Today's update focuses on short-term performance that does not warrant changing our long-term outlook. Shares currently look moderately undervalued,” it said, adding that IBM's long-term AI opportunities come from its hybrid cloud and data software, rather than mainframe-related offerings. On the other hand, Oppenheimer downgraded the IBM stock to ‘Perform’ from ‘Outperform,’ according to an alert on TheFly.
